# 3.1  Formulate predictions from scientific literature

## 1. What mathematical models have been proposed to describe heart rate recovery?

Several mathematical approaches have been used to describe the decrease in heart rate following exercise.

A. Linear model

\\\[ HR(t)=HR_0-kt \\\]

This model assumes that HR decreases at a constant rate over time.

It is relatively simple and can approximate a short section of recovery, but physiological HR recovery is generally nonlinear.

B. Mono-exponential decay model

\\\[ HR(t)=HR\_{\\mathrm{rest}}+A e\^{-t/\\tau} \\\]

This model describes a rapid initial decrease followed by a progressively slower decline.

A smaller \\(\\tau\\) indicates faster recovery, whereas a larger \\(\\tau\\) indicates slower recovery.

C. Bi-exponential decay model

\\\[ HR(t)=HR\_{\\mathrm{rest}} +A_1e\^{-t/\\tau_1} +A_2e\^{-t/\\tau_2} \\\]

This model includes two exponential components:

It provides greater flexibility when recovery has distinct fast and slow phases.

## 2. What physiological mechanisms explain the decrease in heart rate after exercise?

The decrease in HR after exercise is mainly controlled by the interaction between the parasympathetic and sympathetic branches of the autonomic nervous system (ANS).

A. Parasympathetic reactivation (vagal reactivation)

During exercise, parasympathetic influence on the heart is reduced. When exercise stops, vagal activity rapidly increases, slowing the sinoatrial node and reducing heart rate.

- It is particularly important during the initial rapid phase of recovery.

- It contributes to the rapid decrease in HR during the first seconds to approximately the first minute after exercise.

- Faster vagal reactivation is generally associated with faster early HR recovery.

B. Sympathetic withdrawal

During exercise, sympathetic activity increases to support cardiovascular demand. After exercise, sympathetic stimulation gradually decreases.

- It contributes to the slower, prolonged phase of HR recovery.

- The reduction in circulating catecholamines (such as adrenaline and noradrenaline) also contributes to the decline in heart rate.

- Its influence is particularly relevant after high-intensity exercise.

C. Other physiological mechanisms

Other factors also influence HR recovery:

- Baroreflex: helps regulate blood pressure and heart rate as cardiovascular demand decreases.

- Central command withdrawal: the reduction in central motor drive after exercise contributes to the restoration of parasympathetic activity.

- Muscle reflexes: mechanoreflex and metaboreflex activity changes as muscle movement stops and exercise-related metabolites are cleared.

- Thermoregulation: elevated body temperature can maintain an increased heart rate during recovery.

## 3.What are the expected characteristics of the recovery curve?

The HR recovery curve is generally nonlinear and can be divided into two main phases.

Fast phase (early recovery)

- HR decreases rapidly immediately after exercise cessation.

- It is predominantly associated with parasympathetic reactivation.

- The curve has a steep negative slope.

Slow phase (later recovery)

- HR continues to decrease, but at a progressively slower rate.

- It reflects continued parasympathetic influence and gradual sympathetic withdrawal.

- HR gradually approaches its resting level.

## 4.Does the literature suggest that one mathematical model is sufficient to describe the entire recovery period?

Not necessarily. The suitability of a model depends on the duration and characteristics of the recovery data.

A mono-exponential model can describe many HR recovery curves reasonably well, especially over a relatively short recovery period. However, it may not fully capture the different physiological processes occurring during early and late recovery.

# 3.2. Test your predictions using the datasets

## dataset three-hour cardio recording

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(jsonlite)

# 1. Set data directory
data_dir <- "../data/cardio_recovery_3h10m"

# 2. Read the three datasets
pulse <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "pulse.csv"))
acc <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "acceleration.csv"))
rr <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "rr.csv"))

# 3. Read metadata
metadata <- fromJSON(file.path(data_dir, "dataset.json"))

# 4. Inspect the structure
glimpse(pulse)
glimpse(acc)
glimpse(rr)

# 5. Check time ranges
range(pulse$timestamp)
range(acc$timestamp)
range(rr$timestamp)

# 6. Check missing values
colSums(is.na(pulse))
colSums(is.na(acc))
colSums(is.na(rr))
```

```{r}
data_dir <- dirname(pulse_file)

pulse <- read_csv(pulse_file)

acc <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "acceleration.csv")
)

rr <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "rr.csv")
)

glimpse(pulse)
glimpse(acc)
glimpse(rr)
```

extract and visualise heart rate over time

```{r}
# Convert timestamp to minutes
start_time <- min(pulse$timestamp)

pulse <- pulse %>%
  mutate(
    time_min = (timestamp - start_time) / 60000,
    HR = value
  )

# Plot heart rate
ggplot(pulse, aes(x = time_min, y = HR)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Heart Rate During the 3-hour Recording",
    x = "Time (minutes)",
    y = "Heart Rate (bpm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

visualise physical activity

```{r}
# Convert acceleration timestamps
acc <- acc %>%
  mutate(
    time_min = (timestamp - start_time) / 60000
  )

# Calculate acceleration variability in 10-second windows
acc_10s <- acc %>%
  mutate(
    window = floor((timestamp - start_time) / 10000)
  ) %>%
  group_by(window) %>%
  summarise(
    time_min = mean(time_min),
    activity_sd = sqrt(
      sd(x)^2 + sd(y)^2 + sd(z)^2
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot acceleration variability
ggplot(acc_10s, aes(x = time_min, y = activity_sd)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Acceleration Variability Over Time",
    x = "Time (minutes)",
    y = "Acceleration variability (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

generate smooth graphs

```{r}
# Heart rate: 1-minute median
pulse_1min <- pulse %>%
  mutate(minute = floor(time_min)) %>%
  group_by(minute) %>%
  summarise(
    HR_median = median(HR, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Acceleration: 1-minute median
acc_1min <- acc_10s %>%
  mutate(minute = floor(time_min)) %>%
  group_by(minute) %>%
  summarise(
    activity_median = median(activity_sd, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
# Smoothed heart rate
ggplot(pulse_1min, aes(x = minute, y = HR_median)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Smoothed Heart Rate Over Time",
    x = "Time (minutes)",
    y = "Median Heart Rate (bpm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Smoothed physical activity
ggplot(acc_1min, aes(x = minute, y = activity_median)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Smoothed Acceleration Variability",
    x = "Time (minutes)",
    y = "Median Acceleration Variability (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

-  Identify the exercise and recovery periods

  exercise period: 0-60min; transition period: 60-70min, recovery period: 70 mins and after

- Identify the period corresponding to post-exercise recovery

  70-190min

  #### fit and compare models
  
```{r}
# ==========================================
# 1. Prepare recovery data
# ==========================================

recovery <- pulse %>%
  filter(time_min >= 70, time_min <= 190) %>%
  filter(!is.na(HR), !is.na(time_min)) %>%
  mutate(t = time_min - 70)

# ==========================================
# 2. Fit linear model
# HR(t) = b0 + b1*t
# ==========================================

model_linear <- lm(HR ~ t, data = recovery)

# ==========================================
# 3. Fit mono-exponential model
# HR(t) = HR_inf + A*exp(-k*t)
# ==========================================
```


```{r}
model_mono <- nls(
  HR ~ HR_inf + A * exp(-k * t),
```


```{r}
data = recovery,
  start = list(
    HR_inf = 55,
    A = 35,
    k = 0.02
  ),
  algorithm = "port",
  lower = c(HR_inf = 0, A = 0, k = 0.00001),
  upper = c(HR_inf = 150, A = 150, k = 1),
  control = nls.control(maxiter = 500, warnOnly = TRUE)
)

# ==========================================
# 4. Fit bi-exponential model
# HR(t) = HR_inf
#          + A_fast*exp(-k_fast*t)
#          + A_slow*exp(-k_slow*t)
#
# k_fast = k_slow + delta_k
# This ensures k_fast > k_slow
# ==========================================

model_bi <- nls(
  HR ~ HR_inf +
    A_fast * exp(-(k_slow + delta_k) * t) +
    A_slow * exp(-k_slow * t),
  data = recovery,
  start = list(
    HR_inf = 55,
    A_fast = 15,
    A_slow = 25,
    k_slow = 0.003,
    delta_k = 0.04
  ),
  algorithm = "port",
  lower = c(
    HR_inf = 0,
    A_fast = 0,
    A_slow = 0,
    k_slow = 0.00001,
    delta_k = 0.00001
  ),
  upper = c(
    HR_inf = 150,
    A_fast = 150,
    A_slow = 150,
    k_slow = 1,
    delta_k = 1
  ),
  control = nls.control(maxiter = 1000, warnOnly = TRUE)
)

# ==========================================
# 5. Display model summaries
# ==========================================

summary(model_linear)
summary(model_mono)
summary(model_bi)

```
  
```{r}
model_bi$convInfo
```

```{r}
model_mono$convInfo
```
```{r}
coef(model_mono)
summary(model_mono)
```
```{r}
# Linear model
summary(model_linear)

# Compare AIC
AIC(model_linear, model_mono)

# Compare RMSE
rmse_linear <- sqrt(mean(residuals(model_linear)^2))
rmse_mono <- sqrt(mean(residuals(model_mono)^2))

rmse_linear
rmse_mono
```
residual analysis
```{r}
# Calculate residuals
recovery$res_linear <- residuals(model_linear)
recovery$res_mono <- residuals(model_mono)

# Linear model residual plot
ggplot(recovery, aes(x = t, y = res_linear)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals - Linear Model (Dataset 1)",
    x = "Time since recovery began (min)",
    y = "Residuals (bpm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Mono-exponential residual plot
ggplot(recovery, aes(x = t, y = res_mono)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals - Mono-exponential Model (Dataset 1)",
    x = "Time since recovery began (min)",
    y = "Residuals (bpm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


The mono-exponential model successfully converged, and the bi-exponential model failed to converge. The mono-exponential model achieved a slightly lower AIC (10483.72) than the linear model (10486.21), with a difference of 2.49. This suggests a modest improvement in model fit after accounting for model complexity.


comparision
```{r}
rmse <- function(actual, predicted) {
  sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
}

comparison <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Linear", "Mono-exponential", "Bi-exponential"),

  R2 = c(
    summary(model_linear)$r.squared,
    1 - sum(resid(model_mono)^2) /
      sum((recovery$HR - mean(recovery$HR))^2),
    1 - sum(resid(model_bi)^2) /
      sum((recovery$HR - mean(recovery$HR))^2)
  ),

  RMSE = c(
    rmse(recovery$HR, predict(model_linear)),
    rmse(recovery$HR, predict(model_mono)),
    rmse(recovery$HR, predict(model_bi))
  ),

  AIC = c(
    AIC(model_linear),
    AIC(model_mono),
    AIC(model_bi)
  )
)

comparison
```
